Clinical Features Boys with Duchenne muscular dystrophy appear normal at birth. Very early motor milestones are met, but walking is often delayed. The first indications of muscle weakness are clumsiness and inability to keep up with peers. Weakness begins in the pelvic girdle muscles and then extends to the shoulder girdle. Enlargement of the muscles of the lower leg associated with weakness, termed pseudohypertrophy, is often present. The mean age of wheelchair dependence is around 9.5 years. Patients develop joint contractures, scoliosis, worsening respiratory reserve, and sleep hypoventilation as the disease continues to progress. Dystrophin is also expressed in the heart and the CNS. Dystrophin deficiency in cardiac muscle often leads to the development of cardiomyopathy and arrhythmias, particularly in older patients. Cognitive impairment and learning disabilities, presumably due to a functional role for dystrophin in the brain, are also common and sometimes produce intellectual disability. Patients with Duchenne muscular dystrophy often succumb to their disease before the age of 25 or 30 years because of respiratory insufficiency, pulmonary infections, and heart failure despite optimal supportive care. This contrasts with Becker muscular dystrophy, which typically presents in later childhood, adolescence, or even adult life; has slower progression; and may allow a near-normal life expectancy. Cardiac involvement leading to heart failure is a common life-limiting complication. The diagnosis is based on history, physical examination, and laboratory studies. Serum creatine kinase is markedly elevated during the first decade of life due to ongoing muscle damage, and then falls as the disease progresses and muscle mass is lost. Genetic testing provides the ultimate confirmation of the diagnosis, but muscle biopsies can still be helpful in cases with difficult to identify genetic alterations. Limb-Girdle Muscular Dystrophy. Limb-girdle muscular dystrophies are a heterogeneous group of at least 8 autosomal dominant and 23 autosomal recessive entities. Their overall incidence is 1 in 25,000 to 50,000 individuals. As indicated by the name, all forms are characterized by muscle weakness that preferentially involves proximal muscle groups. Both age of onset and disease severity are highly variable. The causative mutations involve genes that participate in diverse cellular functions, making it difficult to discern a unifying mechanism of disease pathogenesis. Based on current knowledge, the implicated genes can be grouped according to the proteins they encode:
Structural components of the dystrophin glycoprotein complex such as the sarcoglycans (Fig. 27.11)
Enzymes that glycosylate α-dystroglycan, a component of the dystrophin glycoprotein complex (see Fig. 27.11)
Proteins that associate with the Z-disks of sarcomeres
Proteins involved in vesicle trafficking and cell signaling
Proteins of seemingly diverse function such as the protease calpain 3, and lamin A/C (which is also mutated in some patients with Emery-Dreifuss muscular dystrophy; see next)

Emery-Dreifuss Muscular Dystrophy (EMD). EMD is caused by mutations in genes that encode nuclear lamin proteins. Clinically, it is marked by a triad consisting of slowly progressive humeroperoneal weakness; cardiomyopathy associated with conduction defects; and early contractures of the Achilles tendon, spine, and elbows. The X-linked form (EMD1) and the autosomal form (EMD2) are caused by mutations in the genes encoding emerin and lamin A/C, respectively, both of which localize to the inner face of the nuclear membrane. It is hypothesized that these proteins help maintain the shape and mechanical stability of the nucleus during muscle contraction. They may also influence gene expression by affecting chromatin organization in the nucleus. How defects in these proteins produce the observed phenotypes is unknown.

Facioscapulohumeral Dystrophy. Facioscapulohumeral dystrophy is associated with a characteristic pattern of muscle involvement that includes prominent weakness of facial muscles and muscles of the shoulder girdle. It is an **autosomal dominant** disease affecting about 1 in 20,000 individuals.
Pathogenesis

The pathogenesis of facioscapulohumeral dystrophy is complex and unique. The disease is linked to epigenetic derepression of the gene encoding the transcription factor DUX4, which is silenced in most somatic tissues and can be toxic in cells such as myofibers. In most cases the derepression is thought to result from mutations in regulatory sequences that lead to altered DNA methylation, chromatin relaxation, and DUX4 transcription in skeletal muscle. In a small proportion of cases the derepression of DUX4 results from mutations in chromatin repressors such as SMCHD1.
Ion Channel Myopathies (Channelopathies)

Channelopathies are a group of inherited diseases caused by mutations affecting the function of ion channel proteins. Most channelopathies are autosomal dominant disorders with variable penetrance. Depending on the channel that is affected, clinical manifestations may include epilepsy, migraine, movement disorders with cerebellar dysfunction, peripheral nerve disease, and muscle disease. The following discussion focuses on those channelopathies with muscle involvement.

Myotonic Dystrophy. Myotonic dystrophy is an autosomal dominant multisystem disorder associated with skeletal muscle weakness, cataracts, endocrinopathy, and cardiomyopathy. It affects about 1 in 10,000 individuals. Myotonia, a sustained involuntary contraction of muscles, is a key feature of this disease, which can be variably classified with muscular dystrophies or channelopathies based on its unique pathogenesis.
Pathogenesis

Myotonic dystrophy is a **trinucleotide repeat** expansion disease that results from CTG expansion in the DMPK gene (type 1, DM1) or CCTG expansions in the CNBP gene (type 2, DM2). The following discussion focuses on the more common DM1 variant. The correlation between the length of expansion and disease severity is not as strong as in some other triplet repeat expansion disorders like **Huntington disease** (Chapter 28) but severe congenital myotonic dystrophy is typically linked to larger repeat sizes. Experimental studies suggest that the skeletal muscle phenotype stems from a “toxic” gain-of-function caused by the triplet repeat expansion. Specifically, the expanded CTG-repeats in the DMPK mRNA transcript appear to bind and sequester muscle splicing regulators. This, in turn, is thought to lead to alternative splicing of several genes including CLCN1, which encodes a chloride channel. It is believed that the resulting deficiency of this chloride channel is responsible for the myotonia; of note in this regard, mutations in CLCN1 itself are linked to congenital myotonia. Insulin resistance and diabetes in DM1 may be the result of alternate splicing of insulin receptor isoforms in skeletal muscle.

Differential expression of other genes and accumulation of transcripts containing the trinucleotide repeat may contribute to other manifestations of this disease. Other Ion Channel Myopathies. Different ion channel myopathies may cause decreased or increased excitability resulting in hypotonia or hypertonia. Disorders associated with hypotonia can be further subclassified based on whether symptomatic patients have elevated, depressed, or normal serum potassium levels and are called hyperkale-mic, hypokalemic, or normokalemic periodic paralysis, respectively. Examples of genes that when mutated lead to periodic paralysis or related disorders include the following:
**KCNJ2:** Mutations affecting this potassium channel cause Andersen- Tawil syndrome, an autosomal disorder associated with periodic paralysis, cardiac arrhythmias, and skeletal abnormalities.
**SCN4A:** Mutations affecting this sodium channel cause several autosomal disorders with presentations ranging from myotonia to periodic paralysis.
**CACNA1S:** Missense mutations in this protein, a subunit of a muscle calcium channel, are the most common cause of hypokalemic paralysis.
**CLCN1:** Mutations affecting this chloride channel cause myotonia congenita. As already discussed, CLCN1 expression is decreased in myotonic dystrophy.

**RYR1:** Mutations in the RYR1 gene disrupt the function of the ryanodine receptor, which regulates calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. RYR1 mutations are linked to a congenital myopathy (central core disease) and to malignant hyperthermia.

The latter is characterized by a hypermetabolic state (tachycardia, tachypnea, muscle spasms, and later hyperpyrexia) that can be triggered by anesthetics, most commonly halogenated inhalational agents and succinylcholine. Upon exposure to anesthetic, the mutated receptor allows increased efflux of calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, leading to tetany and excessive heat production.
Diseases of Lipid or Glycogen Metabolism

Many inborn errors of lipid or glycogen metabolism affect skeletal muscle. These disorders tend to produce one of two general patterns of muscle dysfunction. Some lead to patients presenting with episodic symptoms that are brought on by events like fasting or exercise and can include muscle cramping, pain, or rhabdomyolysis from extensive muscle necrosis. Other metabolic myopathies result in slowly progressive damage akin to a dystrophy without episodic manifestations. Listed here are some examples:

Carnitine palmitoyltransferase II deficiency is the most common disorder of lipid metabolism to cause episodic muscle damage with exercise or fasting. The defect in this disorder impairs the transport of free fatty acids into mitochondria.
Myophosphorylase deficiency (McArdle disease) is one of the more common **glycogen storage diseases** affecting skeletal muscle; it also results in episodic muscle damage with exercise.

Acid maltase deficiency results in impaired lysosomal metabolism of glycogen, glycogen aggregation, and disruption of lysosomal function. Severe deficiency results in the generalized glycogenosis of infancy, Pompe disease (Chapter 5). Milder deficiency can cause a progressive adult-onset myopathy that preferentially involves the respiratory and truncal muscles. Enzyme replacement therapy has been used to treat some affected patients and clinical trials are ongoing for possible gene replacement therapy.
Mitochondrial Myopathies

Mitochondrial diseases are systemic conditions that can affect many organ systems, including skeletal muscle. Many of the causative mutations impair the ability of mitochondria to generate adenosine triphosphate (ATP). The genetics of these disorders are varied and complex.
Pathogenesis

Mitochondrial proteins and tRNAs may be encoded by either the nuclear genome or the mitochondrial genome (mtDNA). While mutations in nuclear mitochondrial genes follow Mendelian inheritance patterns, mutations in mtDNA are maternally inherited, since all of the mitochondria in the embryo are contributed by the oocyte (Chapter 5). In addition, unlike nuclear DNA, which is present in only two copies and is evenly distributed from a mother cell to daughter cells during cell division, each cell contains thousands of mtDNA copies, which are distributed in a random fashion to daughter cells at the time of cell division resulting in heteroplasmy. It is believed that disease results only when a certain threshold of mutated mtDNA copies is exceeded within a substantial fraction of “at-risk” cells (e.g., skeletal muscle cells) in a tissue.
MORPHOLOGY

The most consistent pathologic change in skeletal muscle is abnormal aggregates of mitochondria that are seen preferentially in the subsarcolemmal area of affected myofibers, producing an appearance that is referred to as ragged red fibers (Fig. 27.13). By electron microscopy, morphologically abnormal mitochondria may be seen. Loss of particular mitochondrial enzyme activities characterizes some mitochondrial diseases and may be appreciated by histochemical staining for cytochrome oxidase. Some mitochondrial diseases lack morphologic changes and can be diagnosed only through enzymatic assays or genetic analyses.

Clinical Features

Skeletal muscle involvement can manifest in many ways including weakness, elevations in serum creatine kinase levels, or rhabdomyolysis. Although the anatomic pattern of muscle weakness is variable, involvement of extraocular eye muscles is common and can be a clue to the diagnosis. Indeed, chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia is a common feature of mitochondrial disorders and may occur as an isolated phenomenon or a part of a multisystem syndrome. The reason that extraocular eye muscles are particularly sensitive to mitochondrial disease is uncertain, but it may be that these muscles have exceptionally high requirements for ATP. In line with this idea, extraocular eye muscles have the most mitochondria per mass of any of the body’s muscles.

Due to the complexity of mitochondrial genetics, genotype/phenotype relationships in mitochondrial disorders are not straightforward. For example, a single point mutation in the mitochondrial leucine tRNA gene may produce isolated chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia in one patient and, in another, a much more severe phenotype, mitochondrial encephalomyopathy with lactic acidosis and stroke-like episodes (MELAS). Similarly, deletions in mtDNA may lead to either isolated ophthalmoplegia or to Kearns-Sayre syndrome, characterized by ophthalmoplegia, pigmentary degeneration of the retina, and complete heart block. Myoclonic epilepsy with ragged red fibers and Leber hereditary optic neuropathy are other examples of mitochondrial disease caused by point mutations in mtDNA. Many mitochondrial disorders, such as subacute necrotizing encephalopathy (Leigh syndrome), are remarkably heterogeneous genetically and may be caused by mutations in either mtDNA or the nuclear genome. In the case of Leigh syndrome, causative mutations have been identified in more than 30 different genes, the common feature being that all of the affected genes encode proteins with essential roles in mitochondrial metabolism.
Gene Therapy for Neuromuscular Diseases

Neuromuscular diseases have been a focus of efforts to develop genetic treatment strategies. These must be tailored to the pathogenesis of the specific disease process and in some instances the specific mutation.
Loss-of-function mutations may be treated with gene replacement therapy or gene modulation.

Adeno-associated virus (AAV) has been under investigation to deliver DNA constructs that can replace defective genes. Limitations include a limited packaging capacity of about 4.7 kilobases (the *DMD* gene, for example, has 14 kb of coding sequence). Nonetheless, an AAV vector engineered to deliver a “mini-dystrophin” gene has recently been approved for treatment of boys with **Duchenne muscular dystrophy**. The long-term benefits of such an approach remain to be determined. Other limiting factors are naturally occurring antibodies neutralizing AAV as well as an immune response elicited by viral proteins or by the transgene that is newly expressed in the target tissue. Hepatotoxicity is also a common side effect with AAV gene therapy.

Strategies for gene modulation under investigation or in use for some patients with Duchenne muscular dystrophy are exon skipping using antisense oligonucleotides or drugs promoting ribosomal read-through of nonsense mutations. Exon skipping using antisense oligonucleotides is a mutation-specific approach and is currently available for patients with variants in exons 45, 51, or 53 of the dystrophin gene that disrupt the normal reading frame. In these patients, exon skipping results in the production of a shortened but partly functional protein that can ameliorate the clinical phenotype. Medications promoting ribosomal read-through have achieved approval in Europe for those 10% to 15% of Duchene patients with nonsense mutations.

Knockdown strategies offer a possible approach for patients with dominantly inherited diseases linked to possible toxic gain-of-function and may utilize RNA interference or gene silencing with antisense oligonucleotides. Still farther from clinical implementation are gene correction therapies utilizing CRISPR/Cas9 or similar technologies.
Disorders of Skeletal Muscle
Altered muscle function may stem from neurogenic or primary myopathic processes.
Myopathic disorders are often marked by necrosis and **regeneration** of myofibers.

Inflammatory myopathies are often linked to distinct autoantibodies, clinical presentation, and histopathologic changes and include **dermatomyositis** (DM), antisynthetase syndrome, immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy (IMNM), sporadic inclusion body myositis (sIBM), as well as overlap myositis. This classification has largely replaced the traditional triad of **polymyositis**, dermatomyositis, and inclusion body myositis.
**DM occurs in children and adults.** Distinct clinical subtypes are associated with specific autoantibodies. DM can be a paraneoplastic disease in adults.
A hallmark feature not found in all cases is perifascicular **atrophy**.
Antisynthetase syndrome is associated with distinct antibodies, most often anti-Jo1, and necrotizing changes in a perifascicular distribution.
IMNM is associated with HMGCR or SRP antibodies, is associated with muscle necrosis, and often lacks prominent inflammatory cell infiltrates.
sIBM is a chronic, progressive disease of older patients associated with rimmed vacuoles.

Muscular dystrophies and congenital myopathies result from genetic mutations that disrupt the function of proteins that are important for various aspects of muscle development, function, and regeneration. Some of these diseases present in infancy, others in adulthood. They may be relentlessly progressive or cause relatively static deficits.
Myopathy can result from toxic injury or be the result of metabolic diseases including those of lipid metabolism, glycogen metabolism, and mitochondria.
PERIPHERAL NERVE SHEATH TUMORS

Most benign and malignant neoplasms of peripheral nerve sheaths are composed of cells that show evidence of Schwann cell differentiation. These include three common types: **schwannoma**, neurofibroma, and malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor (MPNST). Peripheral nerve sheath tumors have several unique features. First, they are associated with relatively common familial tumor syndromes, including neurofibromatosis type 1 (*NF1*), neurofibromatosis type 2 (*NF2*), and schwannomatosis. Second, MPNSTs seen in the context of *NF1* are thought to arise through malignant transformation of preexisting neurofibromas. Malignant transformation of a preexisting benign lesion is a common origin for certain carcinomas (e.g., colon cancer) but is unusual in soft tissue tumors.
Neurofibromatosis
Neurofibromatosis Type 1

This is a common autosomal dominant disorder with a frequency of 1 in 3000 individuals. It is a systemic disease associated with nonneoplastic manifestations and with a variety of tumors, including neurofibromas, MPNSTs, gliomas of the optic nerve, other gliomas (Chapter 28), and pheochromocytomas. Other features include intellectual disability, seizures, skeletal defects, pigmented nodules of the iris (Lisch nodules), and cutaneous hyperpigmented macules (café au lait spots). The disease is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the *NF1* gene, located at 17q11.2, which encodes the tumor suppressor neurofibromin. The neoplastic cells in *NF1*-related tumors lack neurofibromin due to biallelic defects of the *NF1* gene. As discussed in Chapter 7, *NF1* protein has GTPase activity that restrains RAS function. In the absence of *NF1*, RAS remains trapped in its active state. The disease has a high penetrance but variable expressivity. Some patients exhibit only subtle features, while others show disease that is restricted to certain parts of the body, a distribution that is attributable to mosaicism. An unfortunate subset has severe disease. Large chromosomal deletions that span *NF1* and extend to involve adjacent genes tend to be associated with more severe phenotypes.
Neurofibromatosis Type 2

This is an autosomal dominant disorder associated with the development of schwannomas, meningiomas, and spinal ependymomas (but not neurofibromas). Bilateral vestibular schwannomas are a hallmark of this disease and are found in many affected patients. This disorder is less common than *NF1*, having a frequency of 1 in 40,000 to 50,000 individuals. Certain other rare familial syndromes are also associated with multiple schwannomas, such as schwannomatosis.

The *NF2* gene is located on chromosome 22q12 and is also commonly mutated in sporadic spinal ependymomas, meningiomas and schwannomas. The *NF2* gene product, merlin, is a cytoskeletal protein that participates in the regulation of several key signaling pathways that are involved in control of cell shape, cell growth, and cell adhesion.
There is some correlation between the type of mutation and clinical symptoms, with nonsense and frameshift mutations causing more severe phenotypes than missense mutations.
Schwannomas

These are benign tumors that exhibit Schwann cell differentiation and arise from peripheral nerves. Schwannomas are a component of *NF2*, and even sporadic schwannomas are commonly associated with somatic inactivating mutations in the *NF2* gene.
MORPHOLOGY

Schwannomas are well-circumscribed, encapsulated masses that attach loosely to the associated nerve without invading it. Grossly, these tumors form firm, gray masses. Microscopically, they are composed of Schwann cells that typically have a spindled elongated nucleus with a wavy or buckled shape. Like normal Schwann cells, the tumor cells express the markers S100 and SOX10 and are surrounded by continuous basement membrane that can be visualized by electron microscopy or immunohistochemistry. Schwannomas typically include regions referred to as Antoni A areas in which the cells are arranged in distinct patterns like streaming fascicles and other areas referred to as Antoni B areas that appear more myxoid and exhibit less distinct architectural patterning (Fig. 27.14A). Palisading of nuclei is common in the Antoni A areas and arrangements with palisading nuclei around central “nuclear-free zones” are termed Verocay bodies (Fig. 27.14B). A variety of degenerative changes may be found in schwannomas, including nuclear pleomorphism, xanthomatous change, vascular hyalinization, cystic change, and necrosis. Some large, mitotically active schwannomas lacking Antoni B areas can mimic a sarcoma.
Clinical Features

Schwann cells are present around the axons in cranial nerves II through XII, nerve roots, large named nerves as well as tiny, distal nerve branches, and schwannomas can occur in all these locations. The presenting symptoms can simply be those of a mass lesion, resulting from compression of the adjacent nerve, or may be related to compression of adjacent CNS tissue. Within the cranial vault, most schwannomas occur at the cerebellopontine angle, where they are attached to the vestibular branch of cranial nerve VIII. Affected individuals often present with tinnitus and hearing loss; the tumor has previously been referred to as an acoustic neuroma—a double misnomer, since the tumor neither arises from the acoustic portion of the nerve nor is it a neuroma. A more recently proposed and preferred name is vestibular schwannoma. Schwannomas typically grow as a mass abutting but not infiltrating a preexisting nerve. Surgical resection is therefore often possible and can be curative. Stereotactic radiosurgery is another treatment option. Schwannomas may recur locally if incompletely resected, but malignant transformation is extremely rare.

Neurofibromas

Neurofibromas are benign nerve sheath tumors that are more heterogeneous in composition than **schwannomas**. The neoplastic Schwann cells are admixed with perineurial-like cells, fibroblasts, mast cells, and CD341 spindle cells. Neurofibromas may be either sporadic or *NF1*-associated. Different types of neurofibroma can be distinguished depending on their growth pattern.
Superficial cutaneous neurofibromas often present as pedunculated nodules that can be seen isolated (if sporadic) or multiple (if *NF1*- associated).
Diffuse neurofibromas often present as a large plaque-like elevation of skin and are typically *NF1*-associated.
Plexiform neurofibromas can be found in deep or superficial locations in association with nerve roots or large nerves and are uniformly *NF1*-associated.
Pathogenesis

Only the Schwann cells in neurofibromas show complete loss of the *NF1* gene product, neurofibromin, indicating that these are neoplastic cells. Haploinsufficiency for the *NF1* gene in other associated cells may also contribute to the growth of *NF1*-associated tumors. For example, there is evidence that *NF1*-haploinsufficient mast cells are hypersensitive to *KIT* ligand produced by Schwann cells and in response secrete factors that stimulate Schwann cell growth. This form of tumor/stromal cell cross-talk may be targetable with inhibitors of the *KIT* receptor tyrosine kinase. Other studies suggest that plexiform neurofibromas and dermal neurofibromas arise from different neural crest–derived precursor cells. Malignant transformation of neurofibroma to MPNST is usually observed in the plexiform variant but is sometimes also seen in the diffuse type. The overall incidence of MPNST in *NF1* patients is about 5% to 10%, but patients with large numbers of plexiform neurofibromas and large deletions in the *NF1* gene are at higher risk.
MORPHOLOGY
Localized cutaneous neurofibroma. These are small, well-delineated but unencapsulated nodular lesions that arise in the dermis and subcutaneous fat.

They have relatively low cellularity and contain bland Schwann cells admixed with stromal cells such as mast cells, perineurial cells, CD341 spindle cells, and fibroblasts. Adnexal structures are sometimes entrapped at the edges of the lesion. The stroma of these tumors contains loose collagen.

Diffuse neurofibroma. This tumor has morphologic features similar to those seen in localized cutaneous neurofibromas but exhibits a distinctly different growth pattern. The tumor diffusely infiltrates dermis, subcutaneous connective tissue, or deep soft tissues, entrapping fat and appendage structures, resulting in large, often plaque-like, lesions. Focal collections of cells mimicking the appearance of Meissner corpuscles (so-called pseudo- Meissner corpuscles or tactile-like bodies) are an associated feature.

Plexiform neurofibroma. These tumors grow within and expand multiple nerve fascicles (Fig. 27.14C), entrapping associated axons. The external perineurial layer of the nerve is preserved, giving individual nodules an encapsulated appearance. The expanded, ropy thickening of multiple nerve fascicles results in what is sometimes referred to as a “bag of worms” appearance upon gross examination. The tumor has a cellular composition similar to that of other neurofibromas. The extracellular matrix varies from loose and myxoid to more collagenous and fibrous. Collagen is often seen in bundles likened to “shredded carrots” (Fig. 27.14D).
Malignant Peripheral Nerve Sheath Tumors

Most malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors (MPNSTs) are high-grade tumors, but low-grade variants are recognized. About half arise in *NF1* patients and are assumed to result from malignant transformation of a plexiform neurofibroma. Sporadic cases may arise *de novo*. Most are associated with larger peripheral nerves in the chest, abdomen, pelvis, neck, or limb-girdle. MPNSTs exhibit complex chromosomal aberrations including chromosome gains and losses. High-grade MPNSTs exhibit genetic or epigenetic abnormalities in addition to *NF1* alterations. These include loss of the polycomb repressor complex PRC2, which is responsible for placing repression marks on histone H3; and trimethylated histone 3; homozygous loss of *CDKN2A*/B, which encodes several tumor suppressor proteins, including the cell cycle regulator p16 and the p53 regulator p14.
MORPHOLOGY

The lesions are poorly defined tumor masses that infiltrate along the axis of the parent nerve and invade adjacent soft tissues. A wide range of histologic appearances can be encountered. Typical cases show a fasciculated arrangement of spindle cells. At low power the tumor often appears “marbleized” due to variations in cellularity. Mitoses, necrosis, and nuclear **anaplasia** are common.

An interesting phenomenon observed in MPNST is described as “divergent differentiation.” This term refers to the presence of focal areas that exhibit other lines of differentiation, including glandular, cartilaginous, osseous, or rhabdomyoblastic morphology. A tumor exhibiting the latter is referred to as Triton tumor. Due to the poorly differentiated nature of MPNST, the distinction from an undifferentiated sarcoma may not be straightforward. Helpful clues include a diagnosis of *NF1* in the affected patient, a clearly demonstrated anatomic relationship to a nerve or to a preexisting neurofibroma, and the presence of molecular changes described above.
Other Types of Nerve Sheath Tumors
There are other tumors that are thought to be derived from Schwann cells or perineurial cells.

Malignant melanotic nerve sheath tumor (MMNST) was formerly referred to as “melanotic **schwannoma**” but is driven by distinctly different genetic changes, particularly PRKAR1A mutations that lead to increased cAMP-dependent signaling. MMNSTs can be associated with Carney complex and are clinically more aggressive than schwannomas.

Granular cell tumor is composed of polygonal cells filled with lysosomes resulting in the appearance of distinctly granular cytoplasm. Most of these form small superficial or mucosal masses. These tumors are associated with genetic changes in genes affecting vacuolar ATPase function.
Perineurioma is a soft tissue lesion that is thought to arise from the perineurial cells that normally surround individual nerve fascicles.
Peripheral Nerve Sheath Tumors
The three common peripheral nerve sheath tumors—schwannoma, neurofibroma, and MPNST—all arise from cells of Schwann cell lineage.
Schwannomas are encapsulated **benign tumors** that can be associated with *NF2*.
Neurofibromas are benign peripheral nerve sheath tumors sometimes associated with *NF1* that can be subtyped as localized cutaneous, diffuse, or plexiform.
MPNSTs can be *de novo* sporadic neoplasms or *NF1*-associated tumors arising through malignant transformation of a (plexiform) neurofibroma.
